The incubation period of the Elf owl (Micrathene whitneyi) is notable for its brevity relative to many other strigiforms. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] have a developmental duration of approximately 24 days [ab = approximately 24 days], a finding consistent with the species' small body size and rapid life-history pace. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge weighing a mere 5 grams [Wwb = 5 grams], an initial mass that underscores the chick's total dependence on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nourishment. This low neonatal mass is typical of small cavity-nesting owls, where the energetic constraint of the clutch is offset by a relatively brief nestling period.

Fledging represents a critical developmental milestone for the juvenile Elf owl, marking the achievement of aerodynamic capacity. Under the elevated thermal conditions associated with active metabolic periods, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], young birds typically depart the nest at around 30.5 days after hatching [tx = around 30.5 days after hatching], although field observations indicate a range of 28 to 33 days depending on food availability. This interval is relatively compressed compared to many larger owl species, a pattern that reflects the selective pressures of a short breeding season in arid environments. Following nest departure, the fledglings remain dependent on their parents for several additional weeks, gradually honing their hunting skills.

The onset of puberty in the Elf owl occurs after the young have completed their post-fledging dependency period and have begun to establish independent foraging territories. Physiological maturation, under the same thermoregulatory regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is generally completed by approximately 91.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 91.5 days after hatching], though documented values in the literature sometimes narrow this window to between 28 and 33 days for the earliest signs of gonadal development. This discrepancy may reflect differences in individual growth rates or environmental influences on the timing of endocrine activation. Reaching sexual maturity at such a young age is unusual among small owls and is likely an adaptation to exploit temporally abundant prey resources in their desert and semi-desert habitats.

Elf owls are characterized by a modest lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] in the wild, a longevity that is often achieved under the physiologically demanding thermal environment of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This maximum recorded longevity is comparable to that of other small, insectivorous owl species and suggests a relatively high extrinsic mortality rate. The time since birth at first brood, again measured under conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is typically 365 days since birth [tR = typically 365 days since birth], indicating that many individuals breed successfully in their first spring following the winter of their hatching year.

Body mass in adult Elf owls exhibits marked sexual dimorphism. Females, which are typically the larger sex, attain an ultimate wet weight of up to 46 grams [Wwi = up to 46 grams], while males reach a maximum of approximately 43 grams [Wwi = approximately 43 grams]. The initial weight of a newly hatched chick is recorded at around 7.3 grams [Ww0 = around 7.3 grams]. Reproductive output is similarly modest; females typically produce a single clutch of 1 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch of 1 to 5 eggs], with only one clutch annually [F_R_i = one clutch annually]. This low fecundity, combined with a small body size, suggests that even minor environmental perturbations can significantly impact annual recruitment.
